opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most important things we get right, honestly, and it's something we've been very deliberate about from the very beginning. Drug design is an incredibly deep field. There are decades of hard-won intuition in medicinal chemistry, in structural biology, in pharmacology, things you just don't pick up from reading papers. And on the other side, machine learning has its own culture: rapid iteration, scale, building general systems rather than solving one problem at a time. If you just put those two groups in the same building and hope for the best, you tend to get a service relationship. The chemists ask for a model, the ML people build it, throw it over the wall, and nobody's really changing how they think.

So what we try to do is build genuinely mixed teams, where the drug designers and the machine learning researchers are sitting together, working on the same problems, with shared goals. The ML folks need to understand why a medicinal chemist would look at a molecule and immediately say, "that's never going to work," even if the binding affinity prediction looks great. Maybe it's a synthesizability issue, maybe it's a toxicity liability, maybe it's just going to be terrible from a pharmacokinetics point of view. That kind of knowledge has to get into how we define the problems and how we evaluate our models. And in the other direction, we want the drug designers to start thinking in terms of what becomes possible when you have models that can predict structures and properties at a scale and accuracy that wasn't available before. It changes which questions you even bother asking.

A big part of it is also creating a shared language. Early on, a lot of time just goes into translation. What does "accuracy" mean to a chemist versus a machine learning researcher? What counts as a meaningful benchmark? What does success look like on an actual program? Once you get alignment on that, things really start to accelerate, because you get this tight loop where models feed into real design decisions, real experimental data comes back, and that informs the next generation of models.

Ultimately, the bet at Isomorphic is that this isn't about bolting AI onto the existing drug discovery process. It's about rebuilding the process from first principles with AI at the core. And you can only do that if you have people who deeply understand both sides working together as true peers.

r001.rationale: The response does not attribute the scarcity of people expert in both fields to AI-driven drug design being new.

r002.rationale: It calls for genuinely mixed teams working on the same problems with shared goals, and contrasts that with isolated teams handing work across a wall.

r003.rationale: It describes each discipline learning to reason from the other's perspective and building a shared language, with examples of chemists considering model capabilities and ML researchers understanding medicinal chemistry judgments.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is really the core of what we're trying to do, and honestly it's one of the things I find most exciting about Isomorphic. When we started, there was this really strong belief that if you want to build something genuinely new in drug design, you can't just have machine learning people throwing models over the wall to medicinal chemists, and you can't have the drug discovery experts treating ML as a tool that lives in some other building. Both of those failure modes are pretty common in the industry.

So the way we think about it is that we want these people sitting together, working on the same problems, day to day. Not separate teams with a hand-off. And what you find is that early on there's a lot of translation happening. A medicinal chemist will look at a molecule the model has generated and say, this would never be made, or this will be metabolized in the liver in five minutes, and the ML person has to understand why, and then ask, okay, how do I encode that? Is that a data problem, is that a loss, is that a constraint in the generative process? And conversely, the ML researcher will show a chemist what the model is actually capable of, and the chemist starts to rethink which questions are even worth asking, because some things that used to be a six-month experimental campaign become a question you can ask the model in an afternoon.

What I think has really mattered is hiring for a certain kind of curiosity on both sides. The drug designers we have are people who are genuinely interested in how the models work and are willing to be challenged on their intuitions, which have been built over decades. And the ML researchers we hire are people who actually care about the biology and chemistry, who want to understand what a potency assay means, not just optimize a number. If you get that mindset right, the organizational stuff mostly takes care of itself.

And the thing that's been quite striking to me is that the best ideas have come out of the friction between the two. You'll be in a room and a chemist will say something that sounds like a complaint about the model, and twenty minutes later it's turned into a research direction that nobody would have thought of from either side alone. So we try to protect that. We try not to over-organize it. Having the AlphaFold lineage from DeepMind gives us a strong foundation on the modelling side, but the end goal is medicines, and that means the whole thing has to be driven by the real problems, which is where the drug design experience is indispensable.

r001.rationale: The response does not attribute a near absence of dual drug-design and machine-learning experts to the newness of AI-driven drug design.

r002.rationale: It says the experts should work together on the same problems day to day, rather than operate in separate teams with hand-offs.

r003.rationale: It describes each discipline translating the other's ideas into its own terms—for example, chemists explaining a molecule's limitations and ML researchers considering how to encode them as data, a loss, or a constraint.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to get people working on the same problem, rather than treating it as a handoff between disciplines. You don’t want the machine learning team to build a model, throw it over the fence, and ask the drug designers to use it. You want the drug designers involved in defining what the model actually needs to do, and the machine learning researchers understanding why those things matter.

That takes a lot of learning in both directions. What makes a molecule useful as a drug is much richer than any single prediction. And equally, understanding what machine learning can now do can change the way you approach a drug design problem.

So I think a lot about creating an environment where people can ask very basic questions of one another. You need deep expertise, but you also need the humility to say, ‘I don’t understand that—can you explain it?’ That’s where you start to develop a shared language, and where the collaboration becomes really productive.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention the scarcity of people who are world-class in both fields or attribute it to AI-driven drug design being new.

r002.rationale: It calls for both groups to work on the same problem and rejects treating their work as a handoff between disciplines.

r003.rationale: It describes learning in both directions and developing a shared language, but does not identify forming intuitions about another discipline in the conceptual language of one’s own as an aim.

sol-6.1.text:
The key is to get people working together on the same problem, rather than having a machine learning team build something and then hand it over to a drug discovery team. You want the medicinal chemists and biologists involved in defining what the model needs to do, and the machine learning researchers understanding why those things matter.

That takes curiosity and humility on both sides. Someone might be an extraordinary machine learning researcher, but they need to be comfortable asking very basic questions about chemistry. And you want drug discovery experts who are willing to think about how these new capabilities could change the way they work.

When that comes together, it’s a really exciting feedback loop. The science shapes the models, and the models open up new scientific questions. That’s the kind of collaboration we’re trying to build.
